questions.text: Explain the n-gram language model and the Markov assumption.
questions.reference_answer: An n-gram language model estimates the probability of a word given the previous n-1 words. It relies on the Markov assumption: the next word depends only on a limited history of the previous few words rather than on the entire sentence. The probabilities are estimated from counts in a training corpus, for example P(w2|w1) = count(w1 w2) / count(w1). N-grams that never occur in training would get zero probability, so smoothing such as Laplace (add-one) smoothing is needed.

rubric.label: Conditional probability of next word
rubric.description: An n-gram language model estimates the probability of a word given the previous n-1 words

rubric.label: Markov assumption
rubric.description: The Markov assumption says the next word depends only on a limited history of the previous few words rather than the entire sentence

rubric.label: Estimated from corpus counts
rubric.description: Probabilities are estimated from counts of word sequences in a training corpus

rubric.label: Smoothing for unseen n-grams
rubric.description: Unseen n-grams get zero probability, so smoothing such as Laplace add-one smoothing is needed

answers.text: An n-gram model predicts each word using only the n-1 words that come right before it. This rests on the Markov assumption: instead of conditioning on the whole history, we assume the next word depends just on a short window of recent words. The conditional probabilities are learned by counting how often word sequences appear in a corpus, e.g. P(cat | the) = count(the cat) / count(the). Because many valid sequences never appear in training, they would get probability zero, so smoothing methods like add-one (Laplace) are applied.

questions.text: What is cosine similarity and why is it used to compare documents?
questions.reference_answer: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors: their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. It ranges from -1 to 1 (from 0 to 1 for non-negative TF-IDF vectors), and higher values mean the documents are more similar. Because it ignores vector length, documents of different lengths can be compared fairly.

answers.text: To compare two documents we turn them into vectors and look at the angle between them: the dot product divided by the product of the two vector norms. A value close to 1 means the documents point in the same direction and are very similar, while 0 means they share nothing. Since only the direction matters and not the magnitude, a long article and a short note on the same topic can still score high.

questions.text: Differentiate between supervised and unsupervised learning.
questions.reference_answer: Supervised learning trains on labelled data, where each input has a known target output. It is used for classification and regression, for example spam detection or house-price prediction. Unsupervised learning works with unlabelled data and finds hidden structure or patterns on its own. It is used for clustering and dimensionality reduction, for example customer segmentation with k-means or PCA.

answers.text: In supervised learning every training example comes with the correct answer, so the model learns a mapping from inputs to known outputs. Typical tasks are classification, like deciding whether an e-mail is spam, and regression, like predicting house prices. Unsupervised learning gets only raw, unlabelled examples and has to discover structure by itself. It is used for grouping similar items, such as segmenting customers with k-means, and for reducing the number of dimensions with PCA.
Supervised learning uses labelled data, while unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data.

questions.text: Explain the role of the attention mechanism in sequence-to-sequence models.
questions.reference_answer: In a basic encoder-decoder model the whole input sentence is compressed into one fixed-length vector, which becomes a bottleneck for long sentences. Attention lets the decoder look at all encoder hidden states at every output step. It computes alignment scores, turns them into attention weights with a softmax and uses the weighted sum of encoder states as a context vector. This greatly improves the translation of long sentences, and the weights show which input words were used for each output word.

rubric.label: Fixed-vector bottleneck
rubric.description: In a basic encoder-decoder model the whole input is compressed into one fixed-length vector, which becomes a bottleneck for long sentences

rubric.label: Decoder sees all encoder states
rubric.description: Attention lets the decoder look at all encoder hidden states at every output step

rubric.label: Weights and context vector
rubric.description: It computes attention weights with a softmax over alignment scores and uses the weighted sum as a context vector

rubric.label: Benefits
rubric.description: This improves translation of long sentences and the weights show which input words were used, giving an alignment

answers.text: Without attention, the encoder has to squeeze the entire source sentence into a single fixed-size vector, and quality drops for long inputs. Attention removes this bottleneck: at each decoding step the decoder can consult every hidden state the encoder produced. It scores how relevant each source position is, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes the weighted average as the context for that step. As a result long sentences are translated much better, and plotting the weights shows which source words each output word aligned to.
Attention lets the decoder focus on different parts of the input sentence at each output step.
Attention helps the model pay attention to important things.
With attention the decoder still only sees one fixed context vector for the whole sentence, and attention does not help with long sentences.

Enc-dec w/o attn: whole src -> 1 fixed vec (bottleneck). Attn: dec looks at all enc hidden states each step; softmax over scores -> weights; weighted sum = context vec. Better for long sents + gives alignment.
Attention is a technique where the encoder hidden states are deleted after each step and the decoder uses a softmax to randomly choose one input word, which makes training faster.

answers.text: Osmosis is the movement of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a semi-permeable membrane.

questions.reference_answer: TCP is connection-oriented and establishes a connection with a three-way handshake before sending data. It is reliable: it guarantees ordered delivery using acknowledgements and retransmission. UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery or order, so it has lower overhead and is faster. UDP suits real-time applications such as video streaming, online games and DNS, while TCP suits web pages, e-mail and file transfer.

rubric.label: TCP is connection-oriented
rubric.description: TCP is connection-oriented and establishes a connection with a three-way handshake before sending data

rubric.label: TCP is reliable
rubric.description: TCP is reliable: it guarantees ordered delivery using acknowledgements and retransmission

rubric.label: UDP is connectionless and fast
rubric.description: UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery or order, so it has lower overhead and is faster

rubric.label: Typical uses
rubric.description: UDP suits real-time applications such as video streaming, online games and DNS, while TCP suits web pages, e-mail and file transfer

answers.text: TCP first sets up a session between the two hosts using a three-way handshake. It then makes sure every segment arrives, in the right order, by numbering segments, waiting for acknowledgements and resending anything that is lost. UDP skips all of this: it just fires off datagrams with no connection and no guarantees, which keeps the header small and the delay low. That is why live video, voice calls and online games use UDP, whereas browsing, e-mail and file downloads rely on TCP.
